Head coach | highlights = * [[Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XXXI|XXXI]]) | statlabel1 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Receptions]] | statvalue1 = 219 | statlabel2 = Receiving yards | statvalue2 = 3,416 | statlabel3 = Receiving [[touchdown]]s | statvalue3 = 23 | regular_record = {{Winning percentage|55|8|record=y}} | playoff_record = {{Winning percentage|4|5|record=y}} | overall_record = {{Winning percentage|59|13|record=y}} | pfr = BeebDo00 }} '''Donald Lee Beebe''' (born December 18, 1964) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former professional [[wide receiver]] who is the head coach of the [[Aurora University#Athletics|Aurora Spartans]]. He previously played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for nine seasons, primarily with the [[Buffalo Bills]]. Beebe played [[college football]] for the [[Western Illinois Leathernecks football|Western Illinois Leathernecks]] and [[Chadron State Eagles|Chadron State Eagles]] and was selected by the Bills in the third round of the [[1989 NFL draft]]. Following six seasons with the Bills, he was a member of the [[Carolina Panthers]] during their inaugural year and played for the [[Green Bay Packers]] in his last two seasons. A member of the Bills teams that lost four consecutive [[Super Bowl]]s, Beebe achieved recognition for preventing an opposing touchdown by forcing a fumble in [[Super Bowl XXVII]], despite the Bills facing an insurmountable deficit. He made two further Super Bowl appearances with the Packers and was part of the team winning [[Super Bowl XXXI]]. Beebe pursued a coaching career after retirement and was hired as Aurora's head football coach in 2019.

'''Donald Clevester Calhoun''' (April 29, 1952 – December 14, 2020) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[running back]] who played for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Buffalo Bills]], [[New England Patriots]].<ref>{{cite web
 |url        = http://www.patriots.com/alumni/index.cfm?ac=alumnibiosdetail&bio=11375&print=yes
 |title      = 44 Don Calhoun RB
 |publisher  = New England Patriots
 |access-date = 2011-01-03
}}{{dead link|date=September 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> and [[Philadelphia Eagles]].  He later played for the [[New Jersey Generals]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL).

Prior to playing in the NFL, Calhoun played football at [[Wichita High School North]] and [[Kansas State University]]. He was selected in the tenth round of the [[1974 NFL draft]] by Buffalo. In 2009, he was inducted into both the Wichita Sports Hall of Fame<ref>{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.wichitahof.com/Inductees.htm
 |title       = Don Calhoun - athlete
 |work        = Inductees
 |year        = 2009
 |publisher   = Wichita Sports Hall of Fame
 |access-date  = 2011-01-03
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110718043041/http://www.wichitahof.com/Inductees.htm
 |archive-date = 2011-07-18
}}</ref> and the Kansas Sports Hall of Fame;<ref>{{cite web
 |url        = http://www.kshof.org/siteresources/apps/records/halloffamer.asp?id=182
 |title      = Don Calhoun
 |work       = Inductees
 |year       = 2009
 |publisher  = Kansas Sports Hall of Fame
 |access-date = 2011-01-03
}}{{dead link|date=September 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> and in 2010, was chosen and awarded entry into the Wichita North High School Hall of Fame.

In 1976, while playing for the New England Patriots, Calhoun led the NFL in rushing yards per attempt, with 5.6.  He rushed for 721 yards that year.

He died on December 14, 2020, at age 68, in [[Derby, Kansas]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thejacksonmortuary.com/obituary/donald-calhoun |title=Donald Clevester Calhoun, Sr. of Wichita, Kansas |publisher=Thejacksonmortuary.com |date= |access-date=2021-01-26}}</ref>

'''Donald Wayne Bass''' (March 11, 1956{{spaced ndash}}October 26, 1989) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played five seasons for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] from 1978 to 1981 and the [[New Orleans Saints]] in 1982. He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Houston]]. He has two living children.  In his four seasons at Houston, Bass caught 105 passes for 1,821 yards and 16 touchdowns.  Bass was selected by the Bengals in the third round of the [[1978 NFL draft]].  

Bass went on to catch 117 passes for 1,580 yards and 13 touchdowns over his first three seasons.  He did not have any regular season receptions in his last two years, though he did catch a touchdown pass in the Bengals 1981 win over the San Diego Chargers in the AFC championship game. He also recovered a fumbled kickoff return in that game. 

In October 1989, Bass was shot and killed by Darrell Billingslea, after Bass allegedly told police to search Billingslea's motel room for drugs.  Billingslea was convicted of killing Bass in 1990 while serving a 25-year prison sentence for another murder.  He was paroled in 2007 and was convicted of a third murder in 2009, resulting in a 50-year prison sentence on top of the 11 years left for the original killings.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://crimeblog.dallasnews.com/2009/07/man-pleads-guilty-killing-form.html/ |title=Man pleads guilty killing former girlfriend while on parole for two murders | Dallas Morning News |access-date=June 2, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140518214804/http://crimeblog.dallasnews.com/2009/07/man-pleads-guilty-killing-form.html/ |archive-date=May 18, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
